In summary, our research is concerned with
the development and validation of a scale to measure the personality trait of self-control.
the development of a new measure of general intelligence, which we have termed the General Intelligence Factor, or g.

the development of a new method for the measurement of the comparative importance of intelligence and certain character traits in the prediction of school success, and with the determination of the relative importance of intelligence and character traits in the total prediction of school success.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the present tests of intelligence, as they are now used, have not been shown to be adequate for the purpose for which they are usually employed, that is, for the selection or rejection of pupils for the higher grades in the public schools, or for the selection or non-selection of pupils for college entrance.

there was no evidence of the presence of a single factor of intelligence in the tests, and that the tests as a whole were not measuring a single general factor, but rather a group of specific factors which could be grouped into three main groups.

the results of the study indicate the following: (1) The correlation between marks and intelligence is about the same in the two grades, and in the two schools; the correlation between marks, intelligence, and character traits, is higher in the higher grades.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we are not justified in concluding that the tests used are not measuring what we believe they are measuring; that the tests are not measuring the same thing in different individuals, and that the test scores are not related to success in school in the manner which we have been led to believe they are.

the results of the tests of character traits, while they do not measure success in school with anything like the same degree of accuracy that the mental tests do, are nevertheless of sufficient value that they should be taken into account in the estimate of the pupil's school standing, and that they are of such value that they may be expected to increase the accuracy of the prediction of future success.

it seems to be possible to make a reasonably accurate estimate of a child's school success by means of tests which measure his intelligence and his conscientiousness, and which take account also of his social and economic status.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we should not underestimate the role of character in success.
the relationship between intelligence and personality traits is not linear, but curvilinear.
we can measure and predict a child's success at school, and we have found a way to do so that doesn't rely on standardized tests.
